57	- Dollar amounts in results.md: round to nearest penny (`.2f`).

61	## Terminology
62	
63	When the runtime wrapper uses `language_mode` (Python-side variable name), the
64	*user-facing* axis is called **language**, never "mode". This covers docs,
65	prompts, report prose, and LLM summaries. The internal field name stays
66	`language_mode` so existing metrics.json readers don't break; everything else
67	says "language" (e.g. "default/Python, bash, powershell, powershell-tool,
68	typescript-bun"). Rationale: "mode" is ambiguous with agent-approval-modes and
69	execution modes; "language" is the concept readers expect.

71	## Repository rules
72	
73	- **No agent-generated `.github/workflows/` at repo root.** Agent workflows only exist inside workspaces under `workspaces/`. The repo's own CI workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) is the exception.
74	- **Never fix agent-generated code.** The benchmark measures autonomous output. Do not manually fix, edit, or patch workflow files in `workspaces/` or `results/*/generated-code/`.
75	- **`runner.py` observes and records, never intervenes** on agent code or errors.
76	- **Workspaces are throwaway.** Don't commit `workspaces/` contents.
77	- **`results/` is committed.** It contains archived metrics, generated code, and transcripts.
78	- **`CLAUDE.md` is only a pointer.** All instructions go in `AGENTS.md`. Never put substantive content in `CLAUDE.md` — it should only reference this file.

80	## Architecture
81	
82	### Key files
83	
84	- `models.py` — single source of truth for model IDs and token pricing. Update here when Anthropic changes prices.
85	- `runner.py` — benchmark harness. Runs agents via `claude -p`, collects metrics, pushes results. Imports from `models.py` and `generate_results.py`.
86	- `generate_results.py` — generates `results.md` reports and updates `README.md`. Can run standalone: `python3 generate_results.py --all`. Each results.md opens with a "Claude Code versions used" line linking to the per-version docs (see `version_docs.py`).
87	- `combine_results.py` — produces cross-run combined reports `results/results_<dirA>__<dirB>[__<dirC>...].md`. Same table layout as per-run reports plus a CLI Version Legend; uses `judge_consistency_report.py` for the JCS section and `conclusions_report.py` for the Opus-max Conclusions prose. Standalone: `python3 combine_results.py <dirA> <dirB> [<dirC> ...]`.
88	- `test_quality.py` — test + deliverable quality evaluation. Structural metrics (always) + panel-of-judges LLM evaluation (`--llm-judge` for test-quality judge, `--deliverable-judge` for workflow+scripts judge). The default panel is Haiku 4.5 + Gemini 3.1 Pro (configured in the module-level `JUDGES` dict). Each judge writes its own per-run cache file; `load_panel_scores(variant_dir, kind)` reads them and returns a mean-aggregated score dict for the reporting layer. Legacy single-Sonnet `*-llm.json` caches still read for backward compat. Imported by `generate_results.py` for the "Test Quality Evaluation" section.
89	- `llm_providers.py` — pluggable LLM provider abstraction for evaluation tasks (see "Adding LLM providers" below). Currently registered: `claude-cli` (pre-authenticated Claude Code CLI), `gemini-cli` (pre-authenticated Gemini CLI, bypasses billing gate), `gemini-api` (google-genai SDK, requires `GEMINI_API_KEY` and a paid-tier Google AI Studio account).
90	- `version_docs.py` — for each unique Claude Code version observed in a run dir's `metrics.json` files, writes `claude-code-<version>.md` with the full system prompt (concatenated from `Piebald-AI/claude-code-system-prompts` at tag `v<version>`), every default-tool description sorted alphabetically, and the slice of `anthropics/claude-code` `CHANGELOG.md` from the lowest CC version observed in any benchmark in this repo through that version. Standalone: `python3 version_docs.py [<run-dir>]`. Caches upstream content under `.cache/cc-versions/` (gitignored). Output files are referenced by name in each `results.md`'s prominent "Claude Code versions used" line.
91	- `benchmark-instructions-v*.md` — per-version specs given to agents during runs.
92	- `hooks/syntax-check.py` — PostToolUse hook for syntax/lint checking.
93	- `Dockerfile.act` — custom act container image with pwsh + Pester pre-installed. Build with `docker build -t act-ubuntu-pwsh:latest -f Dockerfile.act .`. Runner.py auto-detects it and injects `.actrc` into workspaces.
94	- `run-fresh-matrix-*.sh` — per-campaign wrapper scripts that drive multiple sequential `runner.py` invocations (one per model-effort combo) into a single results dir using `--resume`. Use when the matrix needs more than one effort level; `runner.py` accepts a single `--effort` per invocation by design. See `run-fresh-matrix-2026-05-06.sh` for the canonical 8-invocation full-matrix template.
95	- `skills/` — agent skills following [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io/specification) spec.
96	
97	### Adding new trap detectors
98	
99	See the docstring on `_detect_traps()` in `generate_results.py`. Each trap needs:
100	a kebab-case name, detection logic over bash_cmds/console/metrics, a time estimate,
101	and an entry in `trap_applicable_mode` if mode-specific.
102	
103	### LLM vs structural discrepancy checks
104	
105	After every report generation (`python3 generate_results.py --all`), check the
106	"LLM vs Structural Discrepancies" section in each `results.md`. Discrepancies
107	are auto-classified by `_find_discrepancies()` in `generate_results.py`:
108	
109	- **counter-gap**: structural metrics are implausibly low (e.g. 0 tests or 0
110	  assertions while LLM scores high). This means `test_quality.py` is missing a
111	  test pattern. **Fix the counter** — read the generated test files to identify
112	  the pattern the counter doesn't recognize, add it to the appropriate
113	  `_count_*()` function and the detection/classification patterns, add unit
114	  tests, and regenerate. Counter-gap discrepancies should not persist across PRs.
115	- **qualitative**: structural metrics look reasonable but the LLM disagrees on
116	  quality. The report includes the LLM's justification (from the `summary`
117	  field in `test-quality-llm.json`). These are expected and acceptable — review
118	  the justification to confirm it's coherent, then leave them.
119	
120	If a **new counter-gap** appears after changing `test_quality.py`, it's a
121	regression. Fix it before merging.
122	
123	### Combined-report invariants (`combine_results.py`)
124	
125	The combined report (e.g. `results/results_<dirA>__<dirB>.md`) pools
126	runs across multiple source directories. A few layout invariants must
127	hold — changes here have broken the generated markdown before, so
128	`tests/test_combine_results.py` guards them:
129	
130	- **No duplicate `(language, variant_disp)` rows in Tiers or
131	  Comparison.** `aggregate_rows` groups by `(language_mode,
132	  model_short, effort_level)` only. CLI versions pool into one row;
133	  `cli_versions` on the row retains the per-CLI breakdown for the
134	  legend to consume. (Previously the aggregate split by CLI, which
135	  rendered as duplicate-looking rows whose Model column matched.)
136	- **CLI Version Legend schema.** Exactly one CLI version per row.
137	  Columns: `Variant label | CLI version | Tasks | Languages`. `Tasks`
138	  and `Languages` each hold either `All` (pair covered every task /
139	  every language observed in the report) or a comma-sorted subset.
140	  The plural header `CLI version(s)` and comma-joined version cells
141	  are the old layout — do not reintroduce.
142	- **Section order in the body:** Scoring → Conclusions → **Judge
143	  Consistency Summary** → Tiers → Comparison → Per-Run → Notes. JCS
144	  is a top-level `##`, not a `### ` under Notes, because readers
145	  benefit from the panel-health verdict before they consume
146	  rankings.
147	- **Quality-score lookup key.** The per-variant score bucket is keyed
148	  by `(language_mode, _label(m))` which includes the `-cli<ver>`
149	  suffix; aggregate lookups must therefore use `r["variant_with_cli"]`
150	  (not `r["variant"]`). A prior regression where the lookup used the
151	  CLI-less `variant` caused every aggregate Tests Quality / Workflow
152	  Craft cell to render as `—` despite per-run scores being present.
153	
154	### Where the Conclusions prose lives
155	
156	The max-effort Opus `## Conclusions` block is produced **only for
157	the combined cross-run report** (`combine_results.py`), not for
158	per-run `results.md` files. `generate_results.py` still invokes the
159	JCS Summary LLM call (cheap) but passes `speed_cost_input=None` so
160	`conclusions_report.generate_conclusions_from_inputs` short-circuits
161	the Conclusions call. Reasoning: comparing a single run directory
162	against itself doesn't surface tradeoffs worth ~$1 of max-effort
163	tokens per regen — the Conclusions prose only reads as useful when
164	multiple run dirs are being compared.
165	
166	If you need per-run prose for some new purpose, plumb through a
167	separate prompt; do not re-enable the merged Conclusions call at the
168	single-run site.
169	
170	### Judge rationale audit (`judge_audit.py`)
171	
172	The combined report includes a `## Judge Audit Outcomes` section
173	that lists every run where the panel judges span ≥ 4 points on a
174	1–5 scale (i.e. Haiku = 1, Gemini = 5). For each flagged row the
175	audit scans each judge's rationale for concrete file-existence
176	claims (see `MISSING_PHRASES` + file-extension regex) and resolves
177	them against the run's `generated-code/` tree. Drop rule:
178	
179	- One judge contradicted → drop that judge's score; panel mean
180	  becomes the other judge's number.
181	- Both contradicted → drop both; panel mean becomes `—` and the
182	  row is excluded from aggregates.
183	- Neither contradicted → keep both.
184	
185	Verdicts persist as `judge-audit-<kind>.json` next to each run's
186	judge caches. `test_quality.load_panel_scores` consumes the verdict
187	automatically, so the Tiers / Comparison / LLM-as-Judge tables
188	above honor the audit with no extra plumbing.
189	
190	### Per-judge prompt addendums
191	
192	`JUDGES[...]` in `test_quality.py` accepts a `prompt_addendum_tests`
193	key. The test-quality evaluator appends it to the shared rubric for
194	that judge alone, so a model-specific steer (e.g. Haiku's
195	missing-file sanity note) doesn't drag the other judges along.
196	`python3 test_quality.py --rejudge haiku45 <run_dir>` refreshes
197	only that judge's cache — handy after tweaking its addendum.
198	
199	### Combined-report parity with per-run reports
200	
201	Per-run `results.md` carries three top-level sections the combined
202	report does not yet replicate in full:
203	
204	| Per-run section                  | Combined report status |
205	|----------------------------------|------------------------|
206	| `## Failed / Timed-Out Runs`     | Ported (2026-04-21)    |
207	| `## Test Quality Evaluation`     | Partial — structural metrics + panel LLM-as-Judge table ported; Correlation and LLM-vs-Structural Discrepancies sub-tables still absent |
208	| `## Savings Analysis` (Hook / Trap / Cache savings) | **Not yet ported.** Depends on per-run hook telemetry + `_detect_traps` output that aren't currently threaded into `combine_results.py`. Readers needing savings data should drop into the per-run `results.md` for now. |
209	
210	When porting the remaining bits, factor the section builders out of
211	`generate_results.py` into module-level helpers so both entry
212	points share a single implementation — the duplication we'd
213	otherwise accrue would drift the two reports out of sync.
214	
215	### Judge consistency summary (prompt hygiene)
216	
217	`JUDGE_CONSISTENCY_SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT` in
218	`judge_consistency_report.py` forbids unexplained shorthand. If you
219	surface disagreement rows, introduce them with the plain-language gap
220	size (e.g. "the widest disagreements — a judge scoring 1 vs 5, a
221	4-point gap on a 1–5 scale — include …"). Do not coin abbreviations
222	("Span-N", "Δ-N", etc.) that a reader has to decode. Cite specific
223	runs as `task-id-name / language / model-variant` (the same triple
224	the Per-Run table uses).
225	
226	Follow-up analyses of flagged disagreement rows live under
227	`results/analysis/` as dated standalone markdown files (e.g.
228	`judge_disagreement_1-vs-5_2026-04-21.md`). Link them from the JCS
229	section when regenerating if they remain relevant.
230	
231	### Updating model pricing
232	
233	Edit `models.py`. Check https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models and
234	https://www.anthropic.com/pricing. Then run `python3 generate_results.py --all`.
235	
236	### Regenerating reports
237	
238	After changing `generate_results.py`, run:
239	```bash
240	python3 generate_results.py --all
241	```
242	This regenerates `results.md` for every run directory and updates `README.md`.
243	
244	### Adding LLM providers
245	
246	The LLM-as-judge evaluation in `test_quality.py` uses a pluggable provider
247	system defined in `llm_providers.py`. The benchmark runner (`runner.py`) is
248	inherently tied to the Claude Code CLI (it tests CLI-specific features), but
249	the evaluation layer is provider-agnostic.
250	
251	To add a new provider (e.g., Anthropic API, OpenAI, Codex CLI):
252	
253	1. Open `llm_providers.py` and create a class inheriting from `LLMProvider`.
254	2. Implement `is_available()` — return True when the provider can be used.
255	3. Implement `judge(system_prompt, user_message, model)` — return
256	   `{"text": str, "cost_usd": float, "input_tokens": int, "output_tokens": int}`.
257	4. Register it in the `PROVIDERS` dict at the bottom of the file.
258	5. Use it: `python3 test_quality.py --llm-judge --provider your-provider`.
259	
260	See the docstring in `llm_providers.py` for a complete example skeleton.
261	
262	## Before every PR
263	
264	1. **Run all unit tests and verify they pass:**
265	   ```bash
266	   python3 -m pytest tests/ -v
267	   ```
268	   All tests must pass. Do not create or update a PR with failing tests.
269	2. **If you added or changed code, add or update unit tests** in `tests/`.
270	   New functions need test coverage. Changed behavior needs updated assertions.
271	3. Run `python3 generate_results.py --all` and verify no errors.
272	4. **Check for counter-gap discrepancies** in the generated `results.md` files.
273	   If any "Probable counter gaps" appear, fix them in `test_quality.py` before
274	   merging (see "LLM vs structural discrepancy checks" above). Qualitative
275	   disagreements are expected — verify the LLM justification is coherent.
276	5. Verify all import paths work: `python3 -c "from runner import main"`.
277	6. Spot-check a few numbers in results.md against raw metrics.json.
278	7. If you changed architecture or findings, update this file (`AGENTS.md`).
279	8. If you added files or moved things, update the Files table in `README.md`.
280

Same table layout as per-run reports plus a CLI Version Legend; uses `judge_consistency_report.py` for the JCS section and `conclusions_report.py` for the Opus-max Conclusions prose. Standalone: `python3 combine_results.py <dirA> <dirB> [<dirC> ...]`.
- `test_quality.py` — test + deliverable quality evaluation. Structural metrics (always) + panel-of-judges LLM evaluation (`--llm-judge` for test-quality judge, `--deliverable-judge` for workflow+scripts judge). The default panel is Haiku 4.5 + Gemini 3.1 Pro (configured in the module-level `JUDGES` dict). Each judge writes its own per-run cache file; `load_panel_scores(variant_dir, kind)` reads them and returns a mean-aggregated score dict for the reporting layer. Legacy single-Sonnet `*-llm.json` caches still read for backward compat. Imported by `generate_results.py` for the "Test Quality Evaluation" section.
- `llm_providers.py` — pluggable LLM provider abstraction for evaluation tasks (see "Adding LLM providers" below). Currently registered: `claude-cli` (pre-authenticated Claude Code CLI), `gemini-cli` (pre-authenticated Gemini CLI, bypasses billing gate), `gemini-api` (google-genai SDK, requires `GEMINI_API_KEY` and a paid-tier Google AI Studio account).
- `version_docs.py` — for each unique Claude Code version observed in a run dir's `metrics.json` files, writes `claude-code-<version>.md` with the full system prompt (concatenated from `Piebald-AI/claude-code-system-prompts` at tag `v<version>`), every default-tool description sorted alphabetically, and the slice of `anthropics/claude-code` `CHANGELOG.md` from the lowest CC version observed in any benchmark in this repo through that version. Standalone: `python3 version_docs.py [<run-dir>]`. Caches upstream content under `.cache/cc-versions/` (gitignored). Output files are referenced by name in each `results.md`'s prominent "Claude Code versions used" line.
- `benchmark-instructions-v*.md` — per-version specs given to agents during runs.
- `hooks/syntax-check.py` — PostToolUse hook for syntax/lint checking.
- `Dockerfile.act` — custom act container image with pwsh + Pester pre-installed. Build with `docker build -t act-ubuntu-pwsh:latest -f Dockerfile.act .`. Runner.py auto-detects it and injects `.actrc` into workspaces.
- `run-fresh-matrix-*.sh` — per-campaign wrapper scripts that drive multiple sequential `runner.py` invocations (one per model-effort combo) into a single results dir using `--resume`. Use when the matrix needs more than one effort level; `runner.py` accepts a single `--effort` per invocation by design. See `run-fresh-matrix-2026-05-06.sh` for the canonical 8-invocation full-matrix template.
- `skills/` — agent skills following [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io/specification) spec.

### Adding new trap detectors

See the docstring on `_detect_traps()` in `generate_results.py`. Each trap needs:
a kebab-case name, detection logic over bash_cmds/console/metrics, a time estimate,
and an entry in `trap_applicable_mode` if mode-specific.

### LLM vs structural discrepancy checks

After every report generation (`python3 generate_results.py --all`), check the
"LLM vs Structural Discrepancies" section in each `results.md`. Discrepancies
are auto-classified by `_find_discrepancies()` in `generate_results.py`:

- **counter-gap**: structural metrics are implausibly low (e.g. 0 tests or 0
  assertions while LLM scores high). This means `test_quality.py` is missing a
  test pattern. **Fix the counter** — read the generated test files to identify
  the pattern the counter doesn't recognize, add it to the appropriate
  `_count_*()` function and the detection/classification patterns, add unit
  tests, and regenerate. Counter-gap discrepancies should not persist across PRs.
- **qualitative**: structural metrics look reasonable but the LLM disagrees on
  quality. The report includes the LLM's justification (from the `summary`
  field in `test-quality-llm.json`). These are expected and acceptable — review
  the justification to confirm it's coherent, then leave them.

If a **new counter-gap** appears after changing `test_quality.py`, it's a
regression. Fix it before merging.

### Combined-report invariants (`combine_results.py`)

The combined report (e.g. `results/results_<dirA>__<dirB>.md`) pools
runs across multiple source directories. A few layout invariants must
hold — changes here have broken the generated markdown before, so
`tests/test_combine_results.py` guards them:

- **No duplicate `(language, variant_disp)` rows in Tiers or
  Comparison.** `aggregate_rows` groups by `(language_mode,
  model_short, effort_level)` only. CLI versions pool into one row;
  `cli_versions` on the row retains the per-CLI breakdown for the
  legend to consume. (Previously the aggregate split by CLI, which
  rendered as duplicate-looking rows whose Model column matched.)
- **CLI Version Legend schema.** Exactly one CLI version per row.
  Columns: `Variant label | CLI version | Tasks | Languages`. `Tasks`
  and `Languages` each hold either `All` (pair covered every task /
  every language observed in the report) or a comma-sorted subset.
  The plural header `CLI version(s)` and comma-joined version cells
  are the old layout — do not reintroduce.
- **Section order in the body:** Scoring → Conclusions → **Judge
  Consistency Summary** → Tiers → Comparison → Per-Run → Notes. JCS
  is a top-level `##`, not a `### ` under Notes, because readers
  benefit from the panel-health verdict before they consume
  rankings.
- **Quality-score lookup key.** The per-variant score bucket is keyed
  by `(language_mode, _label(m))` which includes the `-cli<ver>`
  suffix; aggregate lookups must therefore use `r["variant_with_cli"]`
  (not `r["variant"]`). A prior regression where the lookup used the
  CLI-less `variant` caused every aggregate Tests Quality / Workflow
  Craft cell to render as `—` despite per-run scores being present.

### Where the Conclusions prose lives

The max-effort Opus `## Conclusions` block is produced **only for
the combined cross-run report** (`combine_results.py`), not for
per-run `results.md` files. `generate_results.py` still invokes the
JCS Summary LLM call (cheap) but passes `speed_cost_input=None` so
`conclusions_report.generate_conclusions_from_inputs` short-circuits
the Conclusions call. Reasoning: comparing a single run directory
against itself doesn't surface tradeoffs worth ~$1 of max-effort
tokens per regen — the Conclusions prose only reads as useful when
multiple run dirs are being compared.

If you need per-run prose for some new purpose, plumb through a
separate prompt; do not re-enable the merged Conclusions call at the
single-run site.

### Judge rationale audit (`judge_audit.py`)

The combined report includes a `## Judge Audit Outcomes` section
that lists every run where the panel judges span ≥ 4 points on a
1–5 scale (i.e. Haiku = 1, Gemini = 5). For each flagged row the
audit scans each judge's rationale for concrete file-existence
claims (see `MISSING_PHRASES` + file-extension regex) and resolves
them against the run's `generated-code/` tree. Drop rule:

- One judge contradicted → drop that judge's score; panel mean
  becomes the other judge's number.
- Both contradicted → drop both; panel mean becomes `—` and the
  row is excluded from aggregates.
- Neither contradicted → keep both.

Verdicts persist as `judge-audit-<kind>.json` next to each run's
judge caches. `test_quality.load_panel_scores` consumes the verdict
automatically, so the Tiers / Comparison / LLM-as-Judge tables
above honor the audit with no extra plumbing.

### Per-judge prompt addendums

`JUDGES[...]` in `test_quality.py` accepts a `prompt_addendum_tests`
key. The test-quality evaluator appends it to the shared rubric for
that judge alone, so a model-specific steer (e.g. Haiku's
missing-file sanity note) doesn't drag the other judges along.
`python3 test_quality.py --rejudge haiku45 <run_dir>` refreshes
only that judge's cache — handy after tweaking its addendum.

### Combined-report parity with per-run reports

Per-run `results.md` carries three top-level sections the combined
report does not yet replicate in full:

| Per-run section                  | Combined report status |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|
| `## Failed / Timed-Out Runs`     | Ported (2026-04-21)    |
| `## Test Quality Evaluation`     | Partial — structural metrics + panel LLM-as-Judge table ported; Correlation and LLM-vs-Structural Discrepancies sub-tables still absent |
| `## Savings Analysis` (Hook / Trap / Cache savings) | **Not yet ported.** Depends on per-run hook telemetry + `_detect_traps` output that aren't currently threaded into `combine_results.py`. Readers needing savings data should drop into the per-run `results.md` for now. |

When porting the remaining bits, factor the section builders out of
`generate_results.py` into module-level helpers so both entry
points share a single implementation — the duplication we'd
otherwise accrue would drift the two reports out of sync.

### Judge consistency summary (prompt hygiene)

`JUDGE_CONSISTENCY_SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT` in
`judge_consistency_report.py` forbids unexplained shorthand. If you
surface disagreement rows, introduce them with the plain-language gap
size (e.g. "the widest disagreements — a judge scoring 1 vs 5, a
4-point gap on a 1–5 scale — include …"). Do not coin abbreviations
("Span-N", "Δ-N", etc.) that a reader has to decode. Cite specific
runs as `task-id-name / language / model-variant` (the same triple
the Per-Run table uses).

Follow-up analyses of flagged disagreement rows live under
`results/analysis/` as dated standalone markdown files (e.g.
`judge_disagreement_1-vs-5_2026-04-21.md`). Link them from the JCS
section when regenerating if they remain relevant.

### Updating model pricing

Edit `models.py`. Check https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models and
https://www.anthropic.com/pricing. Then run `python3 generate_results.py --all`.

### Regenerating reports

After changing `generate_results.py`, run:
```bash
python3 generate_results.py --all
```
This regenerates `results.md` for every run directory and updates `README.md`.

### Adding LLM providers

The LLM-as-judge evaluation in `test_quality.py` uses a pluggable provider
system defined in `llm_providers.py`. The benchmark runner (`runner.py`) is
inherently tied to the Claude Code CLI (it tests CLI-specific features), but
the evaluation layer is provider-agnostic.

To add a new provider (e.g., Anthropic API, OpenAI, Codex CLI):

1. Open `llm_providers.py` and create a class inheriting from `LLMProvider`.
2. Implement `is_available()` — return True when the provider can be used.
3. Implement `judge(system_prompt, user_message, model)` — return
   `{"text": str, "cost_usd": float, "input_tokens": int, "output_tokens": int}`.
4. Register it in the `PROVIDERS` dict at the bottom of the file.
5. Use it: `python3 test_quality.py --llm-judge --provider your-provider`.

See the docstring in `llm_providers.py` for a complete example skeleton.

## Before every PR

1. **Run all unit tests and verify they pass:**
   ```bash
   python3 -m pytest tests/ -v
   ```
   All tests must pass. Do not create or update a PR with failing tests.
2. **If you added or changed code, add or update unit tests** in `tests/`.
   New functions need test coverage. Changed behavior needs updated assertions.
3. Run `python3 generate_results.py --all` and verify no errors.
4. **Check for counter-gap discrepancies** in the generated `results.md` files.
   If any "Probable counter gaps" appear, fix them in `test_quality.py` before
   merging (see "LLM vs structural discrepancy checks" above). Qualitative
   disagreements are expected — verify the LLM justification is coherent.
5. Verify all import paths work: `python3 -c "from runner import main"`.
6. Spot-check a few numbers in results.md against raw metrics.json.
7. If you changed architecture or findings, update this file (`AGENTS.md`).
8. If you added files or moved things, update the Files table in `README.md`.

## Current state (2026-05-08)

### v4 full-matrix benchmark — complete

`results/2026-05-06_173435/` is the canonical current dataset: 280/280 runs
across 7 tasks × 5 modes × 8 model-effort combos, $493.46 + $40.57 panel
eval = $534.03, 38h 35m wall, 278/280 successful (2 failures).
Single-directory, single-CC-version-line (2.1.131 → 2.1.132 mid-run);
supersedes the `results/2026-04-17_004319/` + `results/2026-04-09_152435/`
combined report. Standard panel-of-judges scores populated.

The 8 model-effort combos: `haiku45` (no effort), `opus`/`sonnet` (no
effort), `opus47-1m` at high/medium/xhigh, `opus47-200k` at medium,
`sonnet46-1m` at medium. The 5 language modes: `default`, `bash`,
`powershell`, `powershell-tool`, `typescript-bun`. The 7 tasks: 11, 12,
13, 15, 16, 17, 18 (task 14 archived earlier).

### Key findings vs prior baselines (CC 2.1.114 → 2.1.131/132)

- haiku45 ~21% faster on average (driven by a bash-mode regression-fix
  on the haiku endpoint; bash specifically went 7× faster, while
  powershell got 33% slower).
- opus47-1m-high notably slower and pricier (+21% dur, +28% cost).
  opus47-1m-medium ~24% faster, opus47-1m-xhigh flat. Other variants
  within run-to-run noise.
- The earlier `2026-04-24_202012` partial run was abandoned (had

### Earlier reference runs

- `results/2026-04-17_004319/` — 245 runs, mix of `2.1.112` + `2.1.114`. Used as the haiku45 / opus47-1m / sonnet46-1m baseline.
- `results/2026-04-09_152435/` — 64/64, CC 2.1.97/98/100. Used as the no-effort opus / sonnet baseline.

- `results/2026-04-02_163146/` — v1, 144 runs, same as v2. Had permission-denial artifacts (88% of errors).
- See `design-and-planning-artifacts/` for historical analysis and planning docs.

### Per-CC-version reference docs

Each run dir contains one `claude-code-<version>.md` per CC version

1	# Benchmark Instructions v4 — GitHub Actions
2	
3	**Version**: v4
4	**Date**: 2026-04-09
5	**Purpose**: Measure how well Claude Code agents perform GitHub Actions workflow authoring tasks across different language constraints, with trap-awareness guidance from v3 findings.
6	
7	**Changes from v3**:
8	- Added "Common Pitfalls" section with guidance derived from v3 trap analysis (115min, 15.8% of v3 time lost to traps)
9	- Act container now has pwsh and Pester pre-installed (matching real GitHub runners). Agents still need an install step for workflows that will run on vanilla act, but the benchmarking container already has them.
10	- GHA workflow addendum expanded with `shell: pwsh` guidance for PowerShell mode
11	- All other methodology, tasks, modes, and models are unchanged from v3
12	
13	## Methodology
14	
15	### Overview
16	
17	Each task is executed by a Claude Code agent under 4 different language constraints ("modes") and with 2 different models, yielding **8 runs per task**. Agents receive only the prompt -- no conversation context, no prior results. Each task requires the agent to produce:
18	
19	1. **A script** implementing the task logic in the constrained language
20	2. **Tests** for the script logic using the appropriate framework
21	3. **A GitHub Actions workflow file** (`.github/workflows/<name>.yml`) that integrates the script into a CI/CD pipeline
22	
23	### Models
24	
25	| Model ID | Short Name | Input $/Mtok | Output $/Mtok | Cache Read $/Mtok | Cache Write $/Mtok |
26	|----------|------------|-------------|--------------|-------------------|-------------------|
27	| claude-opus-4-6 | opus | $15.00 | $75.00 | $1.50 | $18.75 |
28	| claude-sonnet-4-6 | sonnet | $3.00 | $15.00 | $0.30 | $3.75 |
29	
30	### Language Modes
31	
32	1. **default** -- No language specified. The agent chooses whatever language it considers best. Baseline.
33	2. **powershell** -- The agent must use PowerShell. Tests with non-default but well-known scripting language.
34	3. **bash** -- The agent must use Bash. Scripts run with `bash script.sh`, tests use `bats-core`. The "is this really just a shell script?" control case.
35	4. **typescript-bun** -- The agent must use TypeScript with Bun runtime. Scripts run with `bun run app.ts`, tests use `bun test` (built-in test runner). Zero-config like Python but typed.
36	
37	### TDD Requirement
38	
39	Every prompt instructs the agent to use **red/green TDD**:
40	1. Write a failing test first.
41	2. Write the minimum code to make it pass.
42	3. Refactor.
43	4. Repeat for each piece of functionality.
44	5. Create mocks and test fixtures as necessary.
45	
46	### GitHub Actions Workflow Requirement
47	
48	Create a GitHub Actions workflow file at `.github/workflows/<task-name>.yml` that uses your script in a real CI/CD pipeline. The workflow must:
49	- Use appropriate trigger events (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch, etc.)
50	- Reference your script correctly
51	- Pass `actionlint` validation (valid YAML, valid action references, correct syntax)
52	- Include appropriate permissions, environment variables, and job dependencies
53	- Actually run successfully when executed locally with `act` (nektos/act) in a Docker container
54	
55	Design your workflow so its steps work in an isolated Docker container -- use `actions/checkout@v4`, install dependencies your script needs, and run it. Avoid steps requiring external services or secrets without sensible defaults.
56	
57	### Workflow Validation
58	
59	Run `actionlint .github/workflows/<task-name>.yml` and fix any errors. `actionlint` is pre-installed. Iterate until it passes cleanly.
60	
61	### All Tests Must Run Through Act
62	
63	Every single test case must execute through the GitHub Actions workflow via `act`. Do NOT test your script directly -- all testing goes through the pipeline.
64	
65	Structure your workflow to accept test fixture data and produce verifiable output. Your test harness must:
66	1. For each test case: set up a temp git repo with your project files + that case's fixture data, run `act push --rm`, capture the output
67	2. Save all act output to `act-result.txt` in the current working directory (append each test case's output, clearly delimited)
68	3. Assert that act exited with code 0 for each case
69	4. Parse the act output and assert on EXACT EXPECTED VALUES -- not just that output appeared, but that it matches the known-good result for that test case's input. For example: if your workflow bumps version 1.1.0 with a feat commit, assert the output contains exactly "1.2.0", not just "a version number"
70	5. Assert every job shows "Job succeeded"
71	
72	The `act-result.txt` file MUST exist when done. It is a required artifact. `act` and Docker are pre-installed.
73	
74	### Workflow Structure Tests (Also Required)
75	
76	- Parse the YAML and check expected structure (triggers, jobs, steps)
77	- Verify the workflow references your script files correctly (paths exist)
78	- Verify actionlint passes (assert exit code 0)
79	
80	### Pre-installed Tools
81	
82	The following tools are pre-installed in the benchmark environment:
83	- **Python 3** with `pytest`
84	- **PowerShell** (`pwsh`) with **Pester** testing framework
85	- **Bun** (TypeScript runtime with built-in test runner)
86	- **Bash** with **bats-core** testing framework
87	- **actionlint** (GitHub Actions workflow linter)
88	- **shellcheck** (shell script static analysis)
89	- **act** (nektos/act — runs GitHub Actions workflows locally in Docker)
90	- **Docker** (container runtime, used by act)
91	
92	The act Docker container also has `pwsh` and `Pester` pre-installed (matching real GitHub-hosted runners). Your workflow's install-powershell step will be a near-instant no-op. You should still include it for portability, but it won't slow things down.
93	
94	Agents should NOT attempt to install these tools -- they are already available.
95	
96	### Syntax/Lint Hooks
97	
98	All runs have PostToolUse hooks enabled that automatically check files on Write/Edit:
99	- `.py` files: `python3 -m py_compile` for syntax errors
100	- `.sh` files: `bash -n` for syntax errors, `shellcheck` for lint
101	- `.ts` files: `bunx tsc --noEmit` for type errors
102	- `.ps1` files: `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer` for PowerShell analysis
103	- `.yml` files in `.github/workflows/`: `actionlint` for workflow validation
104	
105	Diagnostics appear as additional context before the agent's next turn, enabling faster error correction.
106	
107	### Permissions
108	
109	All tool permissions are bypassed (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`). Agents have full access to all tools without approval prompts.
110	
111	### Execution
112	
113	- Tasks run **sequentially** (one at a time).
114	- Each agent runs in an **isolated workspace directory** containing only a copy of this instructions file.
115	- No conversation context or prior run data is passed to the agent.
116	
117	---
118	
119	## Common Pitfalls
120	
121	The following patterns were observed in v3 runs wasting significant agent time. Agents are encouraged to avoid them:
122	
123	### PowerShell: Use `shell: pwsh` in workflow steps
124	
125	When writing GitHub Actions workflow YAML for PowerShell mode, use `shell: pwsh` on your `run:` steps instead of invoking `pwsh -Command "..."` or `pwsh -File ...` from a bash shell. The `shell: pwsh` directive works correctly in act containers and avoids:
126	- Bash parser errors when PowerShell syntax (like `@'...'@` heredocs) leaks into bash
127	- Dollar-sign escaping issues (`\$` needed for every PS variable inside bash strings)
128	- Quoting/visibility problems when passing structured data (JSON) through bash to pwsh
129	- `$MyInvocation.ScriptName` being empty under `pwsh -File` invocation
130	
131	Example -- prefer this:
132	```yaml
133	    - name: Run script
134	      shell: pwsh
135	      run: |
136	        ./MyScript.ps1 -Config config.json
137	```
138	
139	Over this:
140	```yaml
141	    - name: Run script
142	      run: |
143	        pwsh -File ./MyScript.ps1 -Config config.json
144	```
145	
146	### Act: Limit `act push` invocations
147	
148	Each `act push` run takes 30-90 seconds (container startup + workflow execution). In v3, agents that ran `act push` more than twice spent 15+ minutes on repeated debugging loops. Strategy:
149	1. Get the workflow right with `actionlint` first (instant validation)
150	2. Run `act push` once to verify
151	3. If it fails, read the error carefully and fix the root cause before re-running
152	4. Avoid running `act push` more than 3 times total
153	
154	### Fixtures: Design test data up front
155	
156	Agents that wrote, broke, and rewrote test fixtures (4+ fixture-related commands) lost 1-5 minutes per run. Design your fixture data before writing tests -- think through the edge cases once, create all fixtures, then write tests against them.
157	
158	### Test reruns: Fix the code, not the test command
159	
160	Running the same test command 4+ times without changing the underlying code is a signal you're not diagnosing the root cause. Read the error output carefully, identify what's wrong, fix it, then re-run once.
161	
162	### TypeScript: Expect type error hook cycles
163	
164	The `tsc --noEmit` hook catches type errors on every Write/Edit. This is net-positive (53% catch rate) but each fix cycle takes ~12 seconds. To minimize cycles: use explicit types from the start, avoid `any`, and check your types mentally before writing.
165	
166	### Workflow: Validate with actionlint before act
167	
168	`actionlint` runs instantly and catches most YAML/syntax issues. Always run it before attempting `act push`. Agents that needed 3+ actionlint runs to pass wasted time on iterative fixes that could have been caught by reading the error messages more carefully.

# Benchmark Instructions v4 — GitHub Actions

**Version**: v4
**Date**: 2026-04-09
**Purpose**: Measure how well Claude Code agents perform GitHub Actions workflow authoring tasks across different language constraints, with trap-awareness guidance from v3 findings.

**Changes from v3**:
- Added "Common Pitfalls" section with guidance derived from v3 trap analysis (115min, 15.8% of v3 time lost to traps)
- Act container now has pwsh and Pester pre-installed (matching real GitHub runners). Agents still need an install step for workflows that will run on vanilla act, but the benchmarking container already has them.
- GHA workflow addendum expanded with `shell: pwsh` guidance for PowerShell mode
- All other methodology, tasks, modes, and models are unchanged from v3

## Methodology

### Overview

Each task is executed by a Claude Code agent under 4 different language constraints ("modes") and with 2 different models, yielding **8 runs per task**. Agents receive only the prompt -- no conversation context, no prior results. Each task requires the agent to produce:

1. **A script** implementing the task logic in the constrained language
2. **Tests** for the script logic using the appropriate framework
3. **A GitHub Actions workflow file** (`.github/workflows/<name>.yml`) that integrates the script into a CI/CD pipeline

### Models

| Model ID | Short Name | Input $/Mtok | Output $/Mtok | Cache Read $/Mtok | Cache Write $/Mtok |
|----------|------------|-------------|--------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| claude-opus-4-6 | opus | $15.00 | $75.00 | $1.50 | $18.75 |
| claude-sonnet-4-6 | sonnet | $3.00 | $15.00 | $0.30 | $3.75 |

### Language Modes

1. **default** -- No language specified. The agent chooses whatever language it considers best. Baseline.
2. **powershell** -- The agent must use PowerShell. Tests with non-default but well-known scripting language.
3. **bash** -- The agent must use Bash. Scripts run with `bash script.sh`, tests use `bats-core`. The "is this really just a shell script?" control case.
4. **typescript-bun** -- The agent must use TypeScript with Bun runtime. Scripts run with `bun run app.ts`, tests use `bun test` (built-in test runner). Zero-config like Python but typed.

### TDD Requirement

Every prompt instructs the agent to use **red/green TDD**:
1. Write a failing test first.
2. Write the minimum code to make it pass.
3. Refactor.
4. Repeat for each piece of functionality.
5. Create mocks and test fixtures as necessary.

### GitHub Actions Workflow Requirement

Create a GitHub Actions workflow file at `.github/workflows/<task-name>.yml` that uses your script in a real CI/CD pipeline. The workflow must:
- Use appropriate trigger events (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch, etc.)
- Reference your script correctly
- Pass `actionlint` validation (valid YAML, valid action references, correct syntax)
- Include appropriate permissions, environment variables, and job dependencies
- Actually run successfully when executed locally with `act` (nektos/act) in a Docker container

Design your workflow so its steps work in an isolated Docker container -- use `actions/checkout@v4`, install dependencies your script needs, and run it. Avoid steps requiring external services or secrets without sensible defaults.

### Workflow Validation

Run `actionlint .github/workflows/<task-name>.yml` and fix any errors. `actionlint` is pre-installed. Iterate until it passes cleanly.

### All Tests Must Run Through Act

Every single test case must execute through the GitHub Actions workflow via `act`. Do NOT test your script directly -- all testing goes through the pipeline.

Structure your workflow to accept test fixture data and produce verifiable output. Your test harness must:
1. For each test case: set up a temp git repo with your project files + that case's fixture data, run `act push --rm`, capture the output
2. Save all act output to `act-result.txt` in the current working directory (append each test case's output, clearly delimited)
3. Assert that act exited with code 0 for each case
4. Parse the act output and assert on EXACT EXPECTED VALUES -- not just that output appeared, but that it matches the known-good result for that test case's input. For example: if your workflow bumps version 1.1.0 with a feat commit, assert the output contains exactly "1.2.0", not just "a version number"
5. Assert every job shows "Job succeeded"

The `act-result.txt` file MUST exist when done. It is a required artifact. `act` and Docker are pre-installed.

### Workflow Structure Tests (Also Required)

- Parse the YAML and check expected structure (triggers, jobs, steps)
- Verify the workflow references your script files correctly (paths exist)
- Verify actionlint passes (assert exit code 0)

### Pre-installed Tools

The following tools are pre-installed in the benchmark environment:
- **Python 3** with `pytest`
- **PowerShell** (`pwsh`) with **Pester** testing framework
- **Bun** (TypeScript runtime with built-in test runner)
- **Bash** with **bats-core** testing framework
- **actionlint** (GitHub Actions workflow linter)
- **shellcheck** (shell script static analysis)
- **act** (nektos/act — runs GitHub Actions workflows locally in Docker)
- **Docker** (container runtime, used by act)

The act Docker container also has `pwsh` and `Pester` pre-installed (matching real GitHub-hosted runners). Your workflow's install-powershell step will be a near-instant no-op. You should still include it for portability, but it won't slow things down.

Agents should NOT attempt to install these tools -- they are already available.

### Syntax/Lint Hooks

All runs have PostToolUse hooks enabled that automatically check files on Write/Edit:
- `.py` files: `python3 -m py_compile` for syntax errors
- `.sh` files: `bash -n` for syntax errors, `shellcheck` for lint
- `.ts` files: `bunx tsc --noEmit` for type errors
- `.ps1` files: `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer` for PowerShell analysis
- `.yml` files in `.github/workflows/`: `actionlint` for workflow validation

Diagnostics appear as additional context before the agent's next turn, enabling faster error correction.

### Permissions

All tool permissions are bypassed (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`). Agents have full access to all tools without approval prompts.

### Execution

- Tasks run **sequentially** (one at a time).
- Each agent runs in an **isolated workspace directory** containing only a copy of this instructions file.
- No conversation context or prior run data is passed to the agent.

## Common Pitfalls

The following patterns were observed in v3 runs wasting significant agent time. Agents are encouraged to avoid them:

### PowerShell: Use `shell: pwsh` in workflow steps

When writing GitHub Actions workflow YAML for PowerShell mode, use `shell: pwsh` on your `run:` steps instead of invoking `pwsh -Command "..."` or `pwsh -File ...` from a bash shell. The `shell: pwsh` directive works correctly in act containers and avoids:
- Bash parser errors when PowerShell syntax (like `@'...'@` heredocs) leaks into bash
- Dollar-sign escaping issues (`\$` needed for every PS variable inside bash strings)
- Quoting/visibility problems when passing structured data (JSON) through bash to pwsh
- `$MyInvocation.ScriptName` being empty under `pwsh -File` invocation

Example -- prefer this:
```yaml
    - name: Run script
      shell: pwsh
      run: |
        ./MyScript.ps1 -Config config.json
```

Over this:
```yaml
    - name: Run script
      run: |
        pwsh -File ./MyScript.ps1 -Config config.json
```

### Act: Limit `act push` invocations

Each `act push` run takes 30-90 seconds (container startup + workflow execution). In v3, agents that ran `act push` more than twice spent 15+ minutes on repeated debugging loops. Strategy:
1. Get the workflow right with `actionlint` first (instant validation)
2. Run `act push` once to verify
3. If it fails, read the error carefully and fix the root cause before re-running
4. Avoid running `act push` more than 3 times total

Agents that wrote, broke, and rewrote test fixtures (4+ fixture-related commands) lost 1-5 minutes per run. Design your fixture data before writing tests -- think through the edge cases once, create all fixtures, then write tests against them.

Running the same test command 4+ times without changing the underlying code is a signal you're not diagnosing the root cause. Read the error output carefully, identify what's wrong, fix it, then re-run once.

### TypeScript: Expect type error hook cycles

The `tsc --noEmit` hook catches type errors on every Write/Edit. This is net-positive (53% catch rate) but each fix cycle takes ~12 seconds. To minimize cycles: use explicit types from the start, avoid `any`, and check your types mentally before writing.

`actionlint` runs instantly and catches most YAML/syntax issues. Always run it before attempting `act push`. Agents that needed 3+ actionlint runs to pass wasted time on iterative fixes that could have been caught by reading the error messages more carefully.

name: Secret Rotation Validator

# Triggers:
#   - push / pull_request: gate every change through the rotation check.
#   - schedule: a daily cron so secrets are re-checked even with no code changes
#     (rotation status is time-dependent — it can change with no commit).
#   - workflow_dispatch: manual run, with a tunable warning window.
on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *" # every day at 06:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      warning_days:
        description: "Warning window in days (secrets expiring within this many days are flagged)."
        required: false
        default: "14"

# Least-privilege: the validator only reads repository contents.
permissions:
  contents: read

# Avoid piling up overlapping runs for the same ref.
concurrency:
  group: secret-rotation-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

# Deterministic, reproducible inputs. ROTATION_NOW pins the reference "today" so
# the same fixtures always yield the same report regardless of when CI runs.
env:
  CONFIG_PATH: fixtures/secrets.json
  ROTATION_NOW: "2026-06-28"
  WARNING_DAYS: "14"

jobs:
  validate:
    name: Evaluate secret rotation
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    # Expose the summary counters so dependent jobs can gate on them.
    outputs:
      total: ${{ steps.check.outputs.total }}
      expired: ${{ steps.check.outputs.expired }}
      warning: ${{ steps.check.outputs.warning }}
      ok: ${{ steps.check.outputs.ok }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Bun
        uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
        with:
          bun-version: latest

      - name: Install dependencies
        # The validator has zero runtime dependencies; --production keeps the
        # container install a fast, offline no-op while still exercising the step.
        run: bun install --production

      - name: Validate secret rotation
        id: check
        env:
          # Manual runs can override the warning window; otherwise use the default.
          WINDOW: ${{ github.event.inputs.warning_days || env.WARNING_DAYS }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          echo "Evaluating ${CONFIG_PATH} as of ${ROTATION_NOW} (warning window: ${WINDOW} days)"

          # 1) Machine-readable JSON report (printed to the log).
          bun run validate.ts --config "${CONFIG_PATH}" --now "${ROTATION_NOW}" \
            --warning-days "${WINDOW}" --format json | tee report.json

          # 2) Human-readable markdown report -> GitHub Actions job summary.
          bun run validate.ts --config "${CONFIG_PATH}" --now "${ROTATION_NOW}" \
            --warning-days "${WINDOW}" --format markdown >> "${GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY}"

          # 3) Summary counters -> step outputs for the dependent "report" job.
          bun run validate.ts --config "${CONFIG_PATH}" --now "${ROTATION_NOW}" \
            --warning-days "${WINDOW}" --format github >> "${GITHUB_OUTPUT}"

  report:
    name: Rotation verdict
    needs: validate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Emit rotation verdict
        env:
          TOTAL: ${{ needs.validate.outputs.total }}
          EXPIRED: ${{ needs.validate.outputs.expired }}
          WARNING: ${{ needs.validate.outputs.warning }}
          OK: ${{ needs.validate.outputs.ok }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          # Single, easy-to-assert verdict line consumed by the act test harness.
          echo "ROTATION_VERDICT total=${TOTAL} expired=${EXPIRED} warning=${WARNING} ok=${OK}"

          {
            echo "## Rotation verdict"
            echo ""
            echo "- Total secrets: ${TOTAL}"
            echo "- Expired: ${EXPIRED}"
            echo "- Warning: ${WARNING}"
            echo "- OK: ${OK}"
          } >> "${GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY}"

          # Surface urgency as workflow annotations (non-fatal: the pipeline still
          # succeeds so downstream notification steps can run).
          if [ "${EXPIRED}" -gt 0 ]; then
            echo "::warning::${EXPIRED} secret(s) are expired and must be rotated immediately."
          fi
          if [ "${WARNING}" -gt 0 ]; then
            echo "::notice::${WARNING} secret(s) are expiring within the warning window."
          fi

          echo "Rotation check complete."

# Secret Rotation Validator

A small TypeScript/Bun tool that reads a configuration of secrets (name,
last-rotated date, rotation policy, and the services that depend on them),
identifies which secrets are **expired** or **expiring soon**, and emits a
rotation report grouped by urgency. It ships with a GitHub Actions workflow that
runs the check on every push/PR and on a daily schedule.

## How urgency is decided

For each secret:

```
expiryDate      = lastRotated + rotationPolicyDays
daysUntilExpiry = expiryDate - now            (negative ⇒ overdue)
```

| Condition                                   | Urgency   |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| `daysUntilExpiry < 0`                       | `expired` |
| `0 ≤ daysUntilExpiry ≤ warningWindowDays`   | `warning` |
| `daysUntilExpiry > warningWindowDays`        | `ok`      |

All date math is done in **UTC** so results never depend on the machine's
timezone — the same fixtures produce identical reports locally and in CI.

## Usage

```bash
bun run validate.ts --config fixtures/secrets.json \
  --warning-days 14 \
  --format markdown \
  --now 2026-06-28 \
  --fail-on expired
```

| Flag             | Default    | Description                                                        |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `--config`       | _(required)_ | Path to the secrets JSON config.                                 |
| `--warning-days` | `14`       | Secrets expiring within this many days are flagged `warning`.       |
| `--format`       | `markdown` | Output format: `markdown` \| `json` \| `github`.                   |
| `--now`          | today (UTC) | Reference date for the evaluation (`YYYY-MM-DD`). Enables deterministic CI. |
| `--fail-on`      | `none`     | Exit `1` when this urgency is present: `none` \| `warning` \| `expired`. |

**Exit codes:** `0` success · `1` `--fail-on` threshold breached · `2` usage/IO/validation error.

### Config format

```json
{
  "secrets": [
    {
      "name": "AWS_ACCESS_KEY",
      "lastRotated": "2026-01-01",
      "rotationPolicyDays": 90,
      "requiredBy": ["api", "worker"]
    }
  ]
}
```

A bare top-level array is also accepted. `requiredBy` is optional (defaults to `[]`).

### Output formats

- **`markdown`** — urgency-grouped tables, ideal for a GitHub Actions job summary.
- **`json`** — the full report object (summary + grouped secrets), machine-readable.
- **`github`** — `key=value` counter lines (`total`, `expired`, `warning`, `ok`)
  for appending to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`.

## Project layout

```
validate.ts                 # CLI entrypoint (bun run validate.ts ...)
src/
  types.ts                  # domain interfaces
  validator.ts              # pure date math + evaluation + report building
  config.ts                 # parsing & strict validation of the config
  formatters.ts             # json / markdown / github renderers
  cli.ts                    # arg parsing + main() orchestration (injected I/O)
fixtures/
  secrets.json              # sample mixed-urgency config (workflow default)
  secrets-all-ok.json       # sample all-healthy config
tests/                      # bun test suites (see below)
.github/workflows/secret-rotation-validator.yml
```

## Tests (TDD)

Built red/green with `bun test`. The suite has two layers:

1. **Unit tests** (`validator`, `config`, `formatters`, `cli`) — fast, pure-logic
   coverage of every branch, written test-first.
2. **Acceptance tests** (`workflow-structure`, `act`) — parse and lint the
   workflow, then run **every behavioral case end-to-end through the GitHub
   Actions workflow via `act`** (Docker), asserting on exact expected values.
   Each `act` run is appended to `act-result.txt`.

```bash
bun test                 # everything (the act layer needs Docker)
bun test tests/cli.test.ts   # a single fast suite
```

## CI workflow

`.github/workflows/secret-rotation-validator.yml` runs on `push`,
`pull_request`, a daily `schedule`, and `workflow_dispatch` (with a tunable
warning window). It has two jobs:

- **`validate`** — checks out, installs Bun, runs the validator, publishes a
  markdown job summary, and exposes the summary counters as job outputs.
- **`report`** (`needs: validate`) — consumes those outputs, prints a verdict
  line, and raises non-fatal `::warning::`/`::notice::` annotations.

It passes `actionlint` cleanly and runs successfully under `act`.

In the GHA-bench benchmark, the workspace `.actrc` maps `ubuntu-latest` to a
**locally-built** image (`act-ubuntu-pwsh:latest`) that exists only in the local
Docker daemon — it is not in any registry. act defaults to `forcePull=true`, so
a plain `act push` tries to `docker pull` it and fails immediately (in <1s) with:

```
Error response from daemon: authentication required - incorrect username or password
```

`--pull=false` explicitly in any `act push` invocation from a test harness. With
that, act uses the already-present local image. A run that finishes in <1s with
"Job failed" and no container logs is this symptom, not a workflow bug — read the
captured output before re-running (act runs are slow; budget is ~3). See
[[ghabench-act-harness-pattern]].

name: bun-tsconfig-types-bun
description: bunx tsc needs "types":["bun"] in tsconfig or Bun/console globals are "not found"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

For a Bun TypeScript project, running `bunx tsc --noEmit` (the GHA-bench
PostToolUse hook) reports dozens of `Cannot find name 'Bun'` / `Cannot find name
'console'` errors even though `@types/bun` is installed under
`node_modules/@types/bun`. tsc does not auto-include it when invoked via bunx.

**Fix:** add `"types": ["bun"]` to `compilerOptions` in `tsconfig.json`.
`@types/bun` (via `bun-types`) then supplies the `Bun` global, `console`,
`process`, node module typings, and `bun:test` types — tsc goes to exit 0.

Note: `bun test` runs fine regardless (Bun strips types at runtime), so this only
matters for a standalone typecheck / the tsc hook, not for the test gate.

description: Proven pattern for the GHA-bench "all tests through act" requirement (Bun)
metadata:

---

GHA-bench tasks require every behavioral test case to run through the workflow
via `act push --rm`, save delimited output to `act-result.txt`, assert exit 0 +
"Job succeeded" per job, and assert EXACT expected values.

**Proven pattern (TypeScript/Bun):**
- A non-`.test.ts` helper (`tests/act-harness.ts`) with `setupCase(fixtureJson)`
  (mkdtemp + copy project files + write `fixtures/secrets.json`), `runAct(dir)`
  (`git init/add/commit` then `Bun.spawnSync(["act","push","--rm","--pull=false"], {timeout:280_000})`),
  and `runActCase()` that appends delimited output to `act-result.txt`.
- In `tests/act.test.ts`, run the act cases ONCE at **module top level**
  (synchronous spawnSync) and store results, then write many cheap `test()`
  assertions. This sidesteps Bun's 5s per-test/hook timeout entirely — no need to
  thread a long timeout through `beforeAll`.
- Make output deterministic: pin a reference "now" via a workflow `env:`
  (e.g. `ROTATION_NOW`) and a CLI `--now` flag, so fixtures map to known values.
- JSON printed via `| tee file` is guaranteed in act stdout; a workflow
  `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` write also gets echoed by act, so markdown is assertable
  too. Emit one easy-to-grep verdict line from a dependent job.

**Why:** keeps act invocations minimal (one per fixture) and assertions fast,
while satisfying the exact-value + artifact requirements. See
[[act-local-image-pull-false]] for the mandatory `--pull=false`.
